questions.stem: In the Late Bronze Age, the Mycenaean Greeks were ruled from palace centres such as:
options: Athens, Corinth and Sparta as city-states
Knossos, Phaistos and Hattusa
Alexandria, Pergamon and Antioch
Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns
questions.explanation: Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns were major Mycenaean palace sites on the Greek mainland. Hattusa was the Hittite capital in Anatolia, and the Classical city-states and Hellenistic cities came much later.

questions.stem: Linear B tablets from Mycenaean palaces record rations, workers, livestock and goods coming in and going out. This shows that the palace economy was:
options: a redistributive system, with the palace collecting and handing out resources
a market economy, in which prices were set by trade using silver coins
a system of independent farmers who paid no dues to any ruler
a temple economy run entirely by priestesses, without any king or palace
questions.explanation: The tablets show palaces gathering produce and labour and issuing rations and materials, which historians call redistribution. Coinage did not exist in the Bronze Age.

questions.stem: The great power in central Anatolia during the Late Bronze Age, whose capital was Hattusa, was the:
options: Persian Empire
Phrygian kingdom
Hittite Empire
Assyrian Empire
questions.explanation: The Hittites ruled much of Anatolia from Hattusa in the Late Bronze Age, and Troy lay on the western edge of their sphere. Persia and Phrygia rose later, and Assyria was based in Mesopotamia.

questions.stem: Around 1200 BCE many palace centres in the eastern Mediterranean, including Mycenaean sites and the Hittite capital, were destroyed or abandoned. Historians refer to this as:
options: the rise of the Hellenistic kingdoms
the Late Bronze Age collapse
the Greek colonisation movement
the Persian conquest of Anatolia
questions.explanation: The collapse ended the palace civilisations of the Aegean and the Hittite Empire. Causes debated include drought, earthquakes, raiders such as the Sea Peoples and the breakdown of trade.

questions.stem: The site generally identified as Troy is the mound of Hisarlik, in modern:
options: eastern Crete, close to the palace of Zakros
north-western Turkey, near the Dardanelles
southern Greece, near the Gulf of Corinth
northern Egypt, in the Nile Delta
questions.explanation: Hisarlik lies in the Troad region of north-western Turkey, close to the entrance of the Dardanelles (the Hellespont).

questions.stem: Why was Troy's location strategically important in the Bronze Age?
options: It controlled the only overland trade route between Egypt and Mesopotamia
It sat on the Nile and controlled the grain trade of Egypt
It guarded the narrow stretch of sea between Crete and the Greek mainland
It overlooked the entrance to the strait leading from the Aegean to the Black Sea
questions.explanation: Troy stood near the entrance to the Dardanelles, so it could control or profit from traffic between the Aegean and the Sea of Marmara and Black Sea. Its wealth and fortifications reflect this position.

questions.stem: In the Greek legend, the Trojan War began after:
options: the Trojan prince Paris took Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta
the Greek king Agamemnon killed the Trojan king Priam at a feast
the Trojans stole the golden fleece from the city of Mycenae
Achilles abducted the Trojan princess Cassandra from her temple
questions.explanation: Paris carried off Helen, and Menelaus's brother Agamemnon led the Greek army to Troy to recover her. Priam was killed only at the city's fall.

questions.stem: In the myth of the Judgement of Paris, Paris awarded the golden apple to Aphrodite because she:
options: was the mother of his father, King Priam of Troy
promised him the most beautiful woman in the world, Helen
promised to make him the king over all of Asia and Greece
promised him victory in every battle he would ever fight
questions.explanation: Hera offered power and Athena offered wisdom or victory in war, but Aphrodite offered Helen. The story explains why Hera and Athena supported the Greeks.

questions.stem: Which statement about the gods in Homer's Iliad is correct?
options: All the gods support the Trojans because Troy is their sacred city
The gods take no part in the war and simply watch from Olympus
Zeus fights on the battlefield beside Achilles in every major battle of the war
Hera and Athena favour the Greeks, while Aphrodite and Apollo help the Trojans
questions.explanation: The Iliad shows gods taking sides: Hera, Athena and Poseidon help the Greeks, and Aphrodite, Apollo and Ares help the Trojans. Zeus tries to balance fate and the wishes of the gods.

questions.stem: Homer's Iliad covers:
options: the long voyage home of Odysseus and the punishment of his wife's suitors
a few weeks in the tenth year of the war, centred on the anger of Achilles
the whole war from the Judgement of Paris to the burning of Troy
the wooden horse and the sack of Troy, told by Odysseus to the Trojans
questions.explanation: The Iliad focuses on Achilles' anger and ends with the funeral of Hector. The wooden horse and the sack were told in other poems of the Epic Cycle and later by Virgil, and the voyage home is the Odyssey.

questions.stem: The Epic Cycle was:
options: a cycle of Roman plays performed each year at the festival of Troy
a set of early Greek epics telling the parts of the Trojan story not in Homer
a series of Hittite treaties naming each of the kings of the city of Wilusa
a set of Linear B tablets listing the ships sent from Pylos to Troy
questions.explanation: Poems such as the Cypria, the Little Iliad and the Sack of Troy filled in the story before and after the Iliad. They survive mainly in later summaries and fragments.

questions.stem: Homer's poems are usually dated to around the eighth century BCE, while the Trojan War is placed in the Late Bronze Age. Why does this matter for using the Iliad as evidence?
options: It means Homer was an eyewitness who fought in the Trojan War
It shows the Iliad was first written down in Linear B by Mycenaean palace scribes
Centuries of oral retelling mixed Bronze Age memories with later details
It proves Homer invented the story of Troy entirely from nothing
questions.explanation: The poems grew from a long oral tradition, so Bronze Age elements such as boar's tusk helmets sit beside later customs. Historians must sift them rather than accept or reject the whole.

questions.stem: Which British resident of the Troad, who owned part of Hisarlik, dug there before Schliemann and suggested it was Troy?
options: Arthur Evans
Leonard Woolley
Howard Carter
Frank Calvert
questions.explanation: Frank Calvert dug trial trenches at Hisarlik in the 1860s and persuaded Schliemann that it was the site of Troy. Evans, Woolley and Carter worked at Knossos, Ur and the Valley of the Kings.

questions.stem: Heinrich Schliemann's excavations at Hisarlik, which began in 1871, are criticised today mainly because he:
options: kept such full records that later archaeologists could not read them
dug only at night, so that the local workers could not see his finds
cut a huge trench through the mound and destroyed layers he did not want
refused to dig deeper than the Roman level and never reached the Bronze Age
questions.explanation: Searching for Homer's Troy in the lower levels, Schliemann dug a great trench that destroyed much evidence, including from the later Bronze Age city. Recording standards at the time were poor, but his work also proved the mound held a long sequence of cities.

questions.stem: In 1873 Schliemann found a hoard of gold and silver objects that he called 'Priam's Treasure'. Later study showed that it:
options: belonged to Troy VIIa and was hidden at the moment the city fell
came from Troy II, about a thousand years before any likely Trojan War
came from the Roman city of Ilium and had been buried by later settlers
was a set of forgeries made in Athens and planted on the site
questions.explanation: The hoard came from the Early Bronze Age level Troy II, far earlier than the Late Bronze Age setting of Homer's war, so it could not have belonged to Priam. It was taken from Berlin in 1945 and is now in Moscow.

questions.stem: Wilhelm Dorpfeld, Schliemann's architect, identified Homer's Troy with which layer?
options: Troy I, the earliest small fortified settlement
Troy VI, with its massive sloping walls and towers
Troy II, where 'Priam's Treasure' had been found in 1873
Troy IX, the Roman city visited by emperors
questions.explanation: Dorpfeld recognised that the Late Bronze Age Troy VI, with strong walls and fine houses, better fitted Homer's 'well-built' city than Troy II. Troy IX is the Roman city.

questions.stem: Carl Blegen, digging from 1932 to 1938, argued that Troy VI was destroyed by an earthquake and that Homer's Troy was Troy VIIa. What evidence did he cite for Troy VIIa?
options: A Hittite letter found in the ruins that was addressed to Agamemnon
A wooden horse preserved in a pit beside the main gate
Crowded houses, storage jars sunk in floors and a destruction by fire
A gold death mask inscribed with the name of King Priam
questions.explanation: Troy VIIa had many small houses packed inside the walls and storage jars set into floors, as if under siege, and it ended in fire around 1180 BCE. No inscription naming Priam or Agamemnon has been found.

questions.stem: Manfred Korfmann's excavations from 1988 changed views of Troy mainly by showing that:
options: the citadel had never been fortified with walls at any time in the Bronze Age
Hisarlik was a Roman fort with no Bronze Age remains at all
Troy had been destroyed by the Persians rather than the Greeks
a large lower town and defensive ditch lay outside the citadel walls
questions.explanation: Using geophysical survey and excavation, Korfmann's team found traces of a lower town and a ditch, suggesting Troy VI/VIIa was a much bigger city than the citadel alone. The extent of the lower town became part of a public debate.

questions.stem: Why did Korfmann's claims about the size of Late Bronze Age Troy provoke a strong debate with other scholars, such as Frank Kolb?
options: Korfmann claimed to have found Homer's own manuscript of the Iliad
Korfmann denied that Troy had ever existed in the Bronze Age
Critics said the lower town evidence was thin and Troy's importance overstated
Critics showed that Korfmann had been digging at the wrong site in mainland Greece
questions.explanation: Kolb and others said the remains of the lower town were too slight to prove a large trading city, while Korfmann defended his reading. The debate shows how interpretations of the same site can differ.

questions.stem: Which modern method helped Korfmann's team locate buried features of the lower town without digging everywhere?
options: Reading the cuneiform tablets of the Pylos archive
Counting tree rings in the beams of the Roman temple
Magnetometer survey of the ground below the citadel
Radiocarbon dating of the gold in Priam's Treasure
questions.explanation: Geophysical survey, such as magnetometry, detects buried walls and ditches. Radiocarbon dating needs organic material, not gold, and Pylos tablets are in Linear B.

questions.stem: At Mycenae in 1876, Schliemann excavated shaft graves in Grave Circle A containing:
options: Roman coins proving the graves were looted in antiquity
gold death masks, weapons and rich grave goods
the bodies of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra with their names
a library of clay tablets in the Hittite language
questions.explanation: Schliemann found gold masks, jewellery and bronze weapons, and one mask became known as the 'Mask of Agamemnon'. No names were found.

questions.stem: Why do historians reject Schliemann's view that a gold mask from Mycenae showed the face of Agamemnon?
options: The shaft graves date to the 1600s to 1500s BCE, centuries before the war
The mask was proved to be Roman, made for the funeral of the emperor Augustus
The mask was found at Troy, not at Mycenae, so it shows a Trojan
Agamemnon is described by Homer as having been buried at sea
questions.explanation: Grave Circle A belongs to the early Mycenaean period, several centuries before a war placed around the 13th or 12th century BCE. Schliemann read his finds through Homer.

questions.stem: Linear B tablets from the palace of Pylos list groups of women workers with names such as 'women of Miletus' and 'women of Knidos'. Historians use them to suggest that:
options: the tablets record the names of every one of the Greek heroes who fought at Troy
Mycenaean palaces used women from the eastern Aegean, perhaps captives
Trojan women governed the palace of Pylos after the end of the war
Mycenaean women travelled freely to Anatolia to work as merchants
questions.explanation: Ethnic labels for women textile workers point to people taken from the Anatolian coast, which echoes Homer's captive women. The tablets are economic records, not lists of heroes.

questions.stem: Linear B, used on the Pylos tablets, was deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, who showed that it recorded:
options: an early form of Latin
an early form of Greek
the Hittite language
the Minoan language of Crete
questions.explanation: Ventris showed that Linear B wrote Mycenaean Greek. The earlier Linear A of Minoan Crete remains undeciphered.

questions.stem: Hittite texts mention a western Anatolian kingdom called Wilusa and a people called the Ahhiyawa. Many scholars link these names with:
options: Babylon and the Assyrians of northern Mesopotamia
Ilios (Troy) and the Achaeans (Mycenaean Greeks)
Athens and the Spartans of the Peloponnese
Egypt and the Sea Peoples of the Nile Delta
questions.explanation: Wilusa is widely equated with Homer's (W)ilios and Ahhiyawa with the Achaeans, Homer's name for the Greeks. The identifications are strong but not certain.

questions.stem: A Hittite treaty records Alaksandu, a ruler of Wilusa, as a vassal of the Hittite king. Why is this source significant for the Troy debate?
options: It shows that Troy was a Hittite city ruled from Hattusa by governors
It places Wilusa in real Hittite diplomacy, with a ruler named like Alexandros
It proves that the Greeks destroyed Troy in the very year the treaty was signed
It names Helen of Sparta as the wife of the ruler of Wilusa
questions.explanation: Alaksandu resembles Alexandros, Homer's other name for Paris, and places Wilusa in real Late Bronze Age politics. It does not record a Greek war or name Helen.

questions.stem: Euripides's tragedy The Trojan Women, first staged in Athens in 415 BCE, focuses on:
options: the building of the wooden horse and its secret entry into the city
the long journey of Aeneas from Troy to found a new home for his people in Italy
the suffering of Hecuba and the captive Trojan women after the city's fall
the duel between Achilles and Hector outside the walls of Troy
questions.explanation: The play shows Hecuba, Andromache, Cassandra and other women waiting to be handed out as slaves to the Greek leaders. Aeneas's journey is the theme of Virgil's Aeneid.

questions.stem: The Trojan Women was performed soon after Athens had killed the men and enslaved the women and children of Melos. Many historians therefore read the play as:
options: a comedy written to mock the Trojan royal family for Athenian audiences
a comment on the cruelty of war and conquest in Euripides's own time
an accurate record of what happened to Trojan women in the Bronze Age
official Athenian propaganda celebrating the victory over Melos
questions.explanation: The play's focus on the victims of a conquest invites comparison with Melos, so it tells us about fifth-century Athenian attitudes more than about Bronze Age Troy. It is a tragedy, not a comedy.

questions.stem: Archaeologists divide the mound at Hisarlik into nine main layers, Troy I to Troy IX. What does Troy IX represent?
options: The earliest Bronze Age village
The city of Priam's Treasure
The citadel with sloping walls
The Roman city of Ilium
questions.explanation: Troy I is the earliest level and Troy IX the Roman city of Ilium. Priam's Treasure came from Troy II, and the great sloping walls belong to Troy VI.

questions.stem: In a mound such as Hisarlik, the oldest settlement is usually found:
options: at the top, since newer cities sink below older ones
around the edges, because each new city was built inside it
in random order, since every city was dug out completely
at the bottom, with later cities built on its ruins
questions.explanation: By the law of superposition, later layers lie on top of earlier ones. At Hisarlik, later builders also levelled the top of the mound, which removed parts of the Bronze Age layers.

questions.stem: In the Iliad, Helen is shown at Troy as:
options: a cruel queen who rules Troy and orders the war against the Greeks
a prisoner kept in chains until the Greeks free her at the very end
a goddess worshipped in the main temple of the Trojan citadel
regretful and blaming herself, yet treated kindly by Priam and Hector
questions.explanation: Homer's Helen calls herself shameful and wishes she had died, while Priam does not blame her. Later writers judged her very differently, some blaming her and others claiming she never went to Troy.

questions.stem: In the legend, after Troy fell Andromache, the widow of Hector, was:
options: sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles by the Greeks
given as a captive to Achilles' son Neoptolemus
made queen of Troy by the victorious Greek army
sent home to her father with all her wealth
questions.explanation: Andromache was allotted to Neoptolemus, and her young son Astyanax was killed. Polyxena, a daughter of Priam, was the one sacrificed at Achilles' tomb.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the fates of women in the Trojan legend?
options: Greek women were all enslaved by the Trojans when Troy won the long war
Trojan women ruled the city after the Greek army had sailed home
Trojan women became slaves of the victors, while Helen was returned to Menelaus
All women on both sides were freed and given land after the war ended
questions.explanation: Hecuba, Andromache and Cassandra were shared out among the Greek leaders, while Helen, the cause of the war, went home with Menelaus. The contrast is central to plays like The Trojan Women.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the Trojan War is best supported by the archaeological and written evidence?
options: Troy was a real, wealthy city destroyed more than once, but Homer's war is unproven
Excavations at Hisarlik have confirmed every event and every hero described in the Iliad
Troy never existed, so the legend was invented entirely by Homer
Hittite texts give a full account of a ten-year siege by Agamemnon
questions.explanation: Hisarlik shows a strong Late Bronze Age city with destruction layers, and Hittite texts place Wilusa in real politics. No source confirms a ten-year war led by Agamemnon, so most historians accept a historical core at most.

questions.stem: The historian Moses Finley was sceptical about a historical Trojan War. Which argument best reflects that view?
options: Troy VI had no walls, so it could never have resisted any siege
Linear B tablets prove the Mycenaean Greeks never sailed across to Anatolia
Homer lived in Troy and invented the war to praise his city
Homer's world reflects later society, and no text confirms the war itself
questions.explanation: Finley argued that the society in Homer belongs largely to the Dark Age, and that the war cannot be confirmed from sources. Troy VI was strongly walled.

questions.stem: How did later Romans use the legend of Troy?
options: They claimed descent from Agamemnon and held festivals celebrating the fall of Troy
They banned the Iliad as a dangerous Greek book
They believed Troy had been founded by Romulus and Remus
They claimed descent from the Trojan hero Aeneas, as in Virgil's Aeneid
questions.explanation: Romans traced their origins to Aeneas, who escaped burning Troy, and Julius Caesar and Augustus claimed descent from his son Iulus. Virgil's Aeneid gave this story its most famous form.

questions.stem: Which ancient leader is recorded as visiting Troy and honouring the tomb of Achilles before his campaign against Persia?
options: Hannibal of Carthage
Pericles of Athens
Alexander the Great
Darius I of Persia
questions.explanation: Alexander, who saw himself as a new Achilles, visited Troy in 334 BCE at the start of his invasion of the Persian Empire. The visit shows how the legend shaped later leaders' images.

questions.stem: The 2004 film Troy leaves out the gods and shortens the war greatly. How should a historian evaluate it?
options: As more accurate than Homer, because it removes the gods
As worthless for any purpose, since films cannot represent the past
As a modern retelling shaped by film-making, not evidence for the Bronze Age
As a reliable reconstruction of events, since it was based on Korfmann's excavation reports
questions.explanation: The film tells us about modern tastes and how the legend is retold, but it is not a source for Troy. Removing the gods does not make it more accurate, since Homer's poem is itself the main source for the story.
